transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-01
Start: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Alex Mercer (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Martin Hale (Acadia Head of MLOps), Sofia Lin (Acadia Platform Eng), Jordan Reeves (Acadia Finance)

Summary: High-level discovery to map Acadia's latency SLOs, monthly budget constraints (~$15k/month demo number), and tradeoffs between Redwood hosted, dedicated, and private paths. Focus on per-token economics, batching/caching levers, quantization tolerance, and pilot scope. Agreed next steps: Redwood to send pricing spreadsheet + benchmark plan; Acadia to supply sample prompts and procurement timeline.

Topics: SLA targets, per-token unit economics, batching vs latency, KV/prefix cache reuse, dedicated pool sizing, encryption/KMS/residency needs, pilot acceptance criteria.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Mercer: Hey everyone, thanks for squeezing this in. quick around the table? I'll kick off — I'm Alex, AE focused on inference economics.
[00:08] Martin Hale: Martin — Head of MLOps at Acadia. We're standing up a customer-service summarization + routing flow, couple hundred thousand requests a month expected initially.
[00:16] Sofia Lin: Sofia, platform engineering. We'll own deployment and networking, likely VPC peering if we go private.
[00:22] Jordan Reeves: Jordan from Finance, here to map cost to budgets and timelines.
[00:25] Alex Mercer: Cool. Priya from our side will do the deep perf stuff, Priya?
[00:28] Priya Rao: hi all, yeah Priya — I'll be running the benchmark and scoping the pilot.
[00:31] Martin: Great. Quick context: we prototyped with OpenAI during PoC, cost got out of hand when we moved to production traffic. We're looking at three options — hosted Redwood API, reserved dedicated capacity, or private deployment — but must hit p95 < 250ms for interactive chat for our support agents and cap monthly spend near $15k while we scale.
[00:50] Alex: Ok that's helpful. Couple clarifying q's — average prompt length and typical generated token length?
[00:55] Martin: Average input ~120 tokens, generation usually 40-80 tokens. We have a long tail for enterprise parity checks but most are short.
[01:05] Priya: That distribution matters a lot for cost and batching. Small outputs are opportunistic for batching but interactive latency <250ms constrains batch windows.
[01:14] Sofia: We can tolerate 200ms of overhead for network; the rest is model. If batching adds 100-200ms, that's maybe too much.
[01:22] Alex: Right. So from the economics lens — Redwood's hosted per-token prices are lower at scale but you trade off some routing guarantees; dedicated gives reserved throughput and predictable p95s at higher fixed cost; private is the big lift but gives total isolation and maybe lower unit cost if you amortize infra.
[01:40] Martin: What's the typical unit math you'd recommend for a 15k/mo ceiling?
[01:45] Alex: Quick back-of-envelope — if your average request is 160 tokens total (input+output) and hosted price is say $0.0004 per token equivalent, that'd be ~160 * 0.0004 = $0.064 per request. At 200k requests/month that's $12.8k. So very sensitive to model choice and batching.
[02:04] Jordan: That's similar to what we saw in the prototype but we had variable model selection, sometimes larger models for better summaries.
[02:11] Priya: Two levers you can use: batching plus queueing for background tasks (huge wins), and prefix/KV cache for repeated context — if many prompts share a customer context, KV cache reduces recomputation tokens. But for interactive routing you probably can't batch aggressively.
[02:29] Martin: Can you explain KV cache? We've seen it but not sure how to measure savings.
[02:33] Priya: Sure. For transformer-style models there's key-value caches for past tokens in the decoder. If you're doing multi-turn chat or reusing same context prefix, you can cache those KV tensors on the server and only compute new tokens. It reduces compute cost per request dramatically. The caveat: cache hit rates matter and cache eviction policies need to align with your traffic.
[02:52] Sofia: Would that work for our use-case? We have a lot of ephemeral sessions but same agent templates.
[02:57] Priya: Likely yes for template-heavy flows; we should instrument sample prompts to estimate hit-rate.
[03:02] Alex: Another lever is model quantization — many teams run 4-bit or 8-bit variants in prod. That cuts GPU inference cost per token, sometimes with small quality delta. We can recommend model variants based on your eval set.
[03:15] Martin: Any rough numbers for 4-bit? like 30-50% cost drop?
[03:19] Priya: In practice, quantization plus kernel optimizations can be 30-60% cost reduction depending on model. But some outputs degrade on very sensitive prompts.
[03:29] Jordan: From finance side we need headroom. If we try hosted first and it's over budget, can we route to smaller models automatically?
[03:36] Alex: Yes, Redwood supports smart routing and fallbacks. You can set a policy: first attempt high-quality model, if cost threshold or latency spikes, route to cheaper variant. Also region-based routing can affect cost.
[03:46] Sofia: Network/residency is a must — we have EU customers; data residency for stored transcripts is critical. Is that supported on hosted?
[03:52] Alex: Hosted supports region-based tenancy in many cases but if you have strict residency or control needs, dedicated or private offers stronger guarantees with VPC and on-prem options. We can map that in the pilot.
[04:03] Martin: Security checklist — SOC 2, SAML SSO, audit logs, KMS for keys, and egress controls.
[04:10] Alex: Yup we can share SOC 2 docs and our security pack. Private offers customer-managed KMS/HSM. We'll attach that.
[04:16] Priya: For the benchmark: propose a 48-72hr microbench with a mix of 10k requests that mimic your traffic distribution: 80% short chat, 20% longer parity checks. We'll measure p50/p95 latency, tokens per second, and cost per 1k tokens.
[04:31] Martin: that sounds good. We'll provide sample prompts — how do you handle PII in samples?
[04:35] Priya: You can mask or use synthetic but keep distribution shapes — token lengths, schema complexity. We also can sign an NDA for real samples if needed.
[04:43] Jordan: Procurement timeline — if pilot looks good we can move to committed reserved capacity in 6-8 weeks.
[04:48] Alex: Good to know. For reserved capacity, we typically size a dedicated GPU pool to align with peak throughput and then we run autoscaling/burst policies to handle spikes. That changes unit economics — more fixed cost but lower marginal per-token price.
[05:02] Martin: Can you give an example trade-off?
[05:04] Alex: Sure. Say hosted gives you $0.0004/token but with no committed spend. Dedicated with a monthly commit might reduce per-token to $0.00025 when fully utilized, but your committed monthly spend might be $10k for the pool. So your break-even depends on utilization.
[05:19] Priya: Another nuance — caching reduces effective tokens billed. If caching yields 30% fewer tokens for your workload, your effective per-request cost changes and commitment becomes more favorable.
[05:29] Sofia: Are we able to do mixed mode — host low-latency endpoints and route heavy batch work to dedicated?
[05:35] Alex: Absolutely. Many customers run a hybrid: hosted for interactive low-latency usage, dedicated for high-throughput offline jobs. Routing rules in the control plane make that smooth.
[05:45] Martin: What about quantization vs accuracy tradeoffs — we need to maintain extractive answer fidelity for legal transcripts sometimes.
[05:53] Priya: For sensitive legal-grade outputs we'd recommend running those on higher-precision or a validated model; cheaper quantized models can serve drafts or internal reranking. We'll run evals on your legal prompt set to quantify regressions.
[06:05] Jordan: On pricing sheet, can you break down hosted per-token by model family, and show dedicated amortized per-token given utilization levels?
[06:12] Alex: Yes, we'll provide a spreadsheet with scenarios: 40%, 70%, 95% utilization for dedicated pools and hosted tier spend ladders.
[06:18] Martin: For the pilot acceptance criteria, what do you normally recommend?
[06:21] Priya: Common acceptance: p95 <= target latency (you said 250ms) for interactive flows, cost per 1k tokens within X% of estimate (say +/- 20%), and QA pass rate on a set of fidelity checks for legal prompts.
[06:33] Sofia: We might need a small private deployment for residency if sample data includes EU-only transcripts. How quickly can that be stood up?
[06:40] Alex: Private is heavier — setup may be 4-8 weeks depending on networking and approvals. Dedicated reserve is quicker, usually 1-2 weeks once contracts are signed. Hosted is immediate.
[06:50] Martin: If we do dedicated, do we still get observability — token-level cost and per-route dashboards?
[06:56] Priya: Yes, Redwood Console gives per-token breakdown, per-route latency, traces, and model-level dashboards regardless of deployment mode.
[07:03] Jordan: On procurement side, required contract length for dedicated?
[07:06] Alex: We do monthly and annual commit options. Annual gives better price. Pilot can be month-to-month.
[07:11] Martin: What's a realistic pilot spend? We want something under $5k to validate.
[07:16] Alex: For a 48-72hr microbench plus a two-week small pilot we can scope to $2k-$4k depending on model choices. We'll detail scenarios.
[07:25] Sofia: For benchmarking, if Priya runs synthetic load from Redwood infra, will networking skew latency numbers compared to our VPC?
[07:31] Priya: Good point. We'll run both remote hosted benchmarks and, if you go dedicated/private, a VPC-peered bench to measure real-world latencies. The microbench includes a VPC test if we can set up peering.
[07:44] Martin: Any gotchas with tokenization differences across models? We had issues where tokens counted differently between vendors and it messes up cost estimates.
[07:52] Priya: Tokenizer differences are real. We'll normalize costs to token-equivalent and show both raw token counts and converted effective tokens for a given model.
[07:59] Alex: Also note streaming vs non-streaming affects perceived latency. For support agents streaming partial answers often looks faster to users. That's another config to test.
[08:08] Sofia: We will want to test streaming with slower models too to see perceived latency.
[08:12] Priya: We'll include streaming path in bench.
[08:15] Martin: Ok let's recap — you will send pricing sheet and pilot proposal; Priya will produce bench plan; we will provide sample prompts and confirm target SLAs and budget.
[08:24] Alex: Yep. Action items and deadlines in the notes. Anything else?
[08:28] Jordan: One more ask — please include amortized data egress charges in the spreadsheet.
[08:32] Alex: Will do.
[08:34] Sofia: And include a short note on SSO + SCIM timeline for integration.
[08:38] Alex: Yup.
[08:40] Martin: Great — thanks. Look forward to the pilot plan.
[08:44] Alex: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with links to docs and the spreadsheet by Friday.

End of meeting.
